# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is the road that leads to the other one.

*Cardinal* argues that a single stretch of the San Francisco Peninsula has held
the controlling position in the American economy for a hundred and forty years,
and that the mechanism doing the holding is older than the place. *Dawn* is the
account of where that mechanism came from — the three thousand years of empire,
collapse, and reinvention that were already finished by the time a Spanish
expedition reached Alta California in 1769.

It is called *An American Odyssey* because it is a journey westward and because
the destination is not a place but a pattern. Whoever controls the passage that
everything must move through sets the terms for everyone else; the passage is
usually built with public effort and captured as private property; and the people
who end up holding it are reproduced by the same institutions across generations.
That is the argument of the companion volume. This one shows the argument being
rehearsed, in different costume, from the eastern Mediterranean to the printing
houses of Florence to the edge of the Pacific.

You do not need to read *Dawn* to read *Cardinal*. *Cardinal* assumes it. But the
Peninsula's story is not the first time any of this has happened, and the reader
who wants to know why California's mechanism felt inevitable the moment it
appeared will find the answer here, several civilisations early.
